params.question: A 9-year-old girl presents with pubic hair but no breast development. Based on the physiology of puberty, which process most likely accounts for her pubic hair?

answers.text: Activation of the HPO axis leading to ovarian oestradiol production

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HPO axis activation (gonadarche) drives breast development via oestradiol. Isolated pubic hair without thelarche suggests the HPO axis is not yet active.

answers.text: Release of adrenal androgens independent of the pituitary-ovarian axis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Adrenarche — the release of adrenal androgens — drives pubic and axillary hair growth. It occurs roughly two years before gonadarche and is entirely independent of the HPO axis.

answers.text: Premature pulsatile GnRH secretion from KNDy neurons

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Premature GnRH pulsatility would activate the entire HPO axis, producing breast development alongside pubic hair — not isolated pubic hair.
Elevated FSH would stimulate ovarian oestradiol, causing breast development as the earliest gonadal sign. Isolated pubic hair without thelarche points to adrenal, not ovarian, androgens.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: adrenarche (adrenal androgens → pubic hair) and gonadarche (HPO axis → breast development) are independent processes. Adrenarche typically precedes gonadarche by about two years.
Well done. Adrenarche and gonadarche are separate processes — adrenarche drives pubic hair via adrenal androgens, while gonadarche drives breast development via the HPO axis.

params.question: A 6-year-old girl presents with breast development and accelerated growth. Her serum LH and FSH are both suppressed. What does this gonadotrophin pattern indicate about the source of her pubertal changes?

answers.text: The HPO axis has been prematurely activated by KNDy neurons

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Central (true) precocious puberty shows elevated or pubertal-range LH and FSH, because the axis itself is driving the process. Suppressed gonadotrophins rule this out.

answers.text: Sex steroids are being produced autonomously, independent of pituitary control

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Suppressed LH and FSH with pubertal signs indicate peripheral precocious puberty — sex steroids are coming from an autonomous source (e.g. ovarian cyst, tumour, or McCune-Albright syndrome), suppressing pituitary gonadotrophins via negative feedback.

answers.text: She has constitutional delay with benign premature thelarche

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Constitutional delay presents as late puberty, not early. Premature thelarche is isolated breast development without accelerated growth and does not suppress gonadotrophins.

answers.text: The low gonadotrophins confirm primary ovarian failure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Primary ovarian failure produces elevated gonadotrophins, because absent ovarian feedback removes the brake on LH and FSH secretion — the opposite of what is seen here.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key principle: in precocious puberty, suppressed LH/FSH means sex steroids are coming from outside the HPO axis (peripheral). Elevated LH/FSH means the axis itself is prematurely active (central). This single result shapes the entire treatment approach.
Exactly right. The central-vs-peripheral distinction hinges on gonadotrophin levels: elevated in central precocious puberty (axis activated), suppressed in peripheral (autonomous sex steroid source).

params.question: A 14-year-old girl with primary amenorrhoea has short stature, a webbed neck, and elevated FSH levels. Which management approach is most appropriate?

answers.text: Reassurance and watchful waiting, as puberty will occur spontaneously

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This suits constitutional delay, where puberty is simply late but will occur on its own. Elevated FSH with stigmata of Turner syndrome indicates gonadal failure — spontaneous puberty will not happen.

Pulsatile GnRH therapy is used for Kallmann syndrome, where the problem is deficient hypothalamic GnRH secretion. In Turner syndrome, the ovaries themselves have failed, so stimulating the pituitary cannot help.

answers.text: Gradual oestrogen replacement timed to bone age, with growth hormone and cardiac surveillance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Turner syndrome requires multidisciplinary care: gradual oestrogen replacement starting around age 12–13 (guided by bone age) to induce puberty, growth hormone to optimise final height, and lifelong cardiac and thyroid monitoring.

answers.text: Surgical drainage of trapped menstrual blood from an imperforate hymen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Imperforate hymen causes outflow obstruction with cyclical pain and haematocolpos, but the girl would show normal pubertal development and normal gonadotrophins — not elevated FSH or short stature.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: elevated FSH + short stature + webbed neck = Turner syndrome. Management is gradual oestrogen replacement (timed to bone age), growth hormone, and cardiac/thyroid monitoring — not watchful waiting or GnRH therapy.
Correct. Turner syndrome demands a multidisciplinary approach: gradual oestrogen for puberty induction, growth hormone for stature, and lifelong cardiac and thyroid surveillance.

interactions.label: An 8-year-old girl with McCune-Albright syndrome has breast development and supp

params.question: An 8-year-old girl with McCune-Albright syndrome has breast development and suppressed LH/FSH levels. Why would GnRH analogues be ineffective in managing her precocious puberty?

answers.text: McCune-Albright syndrome causes resistance to GnRH at the pituitary receptor level

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The issue is not receptor resistance. GnRH analogues work by downregulating pituitary GnRH receptors — which only helps when the pituitary is actively driving the process, not when it is already suppressed.

answers.text: Her HPO axis is already suppressed; oestrogen is being produced autonomously by the ovaries

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In McCune-Albright syndrome, ovarian cysts produce oestrogen autonomously (peripheral precocious puberty). The HPO axis is already shut down by negative feedback, so GnRH analogues have nothing left to suppress.

answers.text: Continuous GnRH delivery paradoxically accelerates pubertal progression in this condition

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Continuous GnRH actually downregulates receptors and suppresses the axis — that is precisely how GnRH analogues work in central precocious puberty. The problem here is that the axis is not the source of sex steroids.

answers.text: GnRH analogues are only effective in children younger than six years of age

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no age cutoff for GnRH analogue efficacy. They work at any age for central precocious puberty. The issue in McCune-Albright is the peripheral mechanism, not the child's age.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key concept: GnRH analogues suppress the HPO axis. In peripheral precocious puberty like McCune-Albright, the axis is already suppressed because oestrogen comes from an autonomous ovarian source. Treatment must target that source directly.

Well done. GnRH analogues suppress a prematurely active HPO axis (central precocious puberty), but cannot address autonomous hormone production (peripheral). McCune-Albright needs targeted therapy to block the autonomous oestrogen source.
